title: What is a skills-based organization?
description: A skills-based organization hires, deploys and develops people on verified skills, not job titles or degrees. What it requires, with OPM and WEF examples.
shortAnswer: A skills-based organization is one that uses skills, rather than job titles, degrees or years of experience, as the main basis for hiring, deploying, developing and promoting people. It describes work as sets of skills, keeps a shared skills language, and relies on evidence of what people can actually do. The approach is also called skills-first; the World Economic Forum and the US Office of Personnel Management both promote versions of it.
keyTakeaways: A skills-based organization treats skills as the unit of talent decisions, alongside or instead of jobs and credentials.
It depends on two foundations: a common skills language (taxonomy or framework) and trustworthy evidence that people hold the skills.
The World Economic Forum describes skills-first as emphasizing skills and competencies rather than degrees, job histories or job titles.
US federal hiring policy is an example in practice: the Merit Hiring Plan directs agencies to replace self-assessment ranking with technical and alternative assessments.
Self-reported skills are the weakest evidence; skills-based decisions are only as good as the assessment behind them.

sections.heading: What does skills-based mean in practice?

blocks.text: Skills-based means that talent decisions start from the skills the work requires and the skills a person can demonstrate. The World Economic Forum (WEF) white paper [Putting Skills First: A Framework for Action](https://www.weforum.org/publications/putting-skills-first-a-framework-for-action/) (May 2023) describes skills-first as an approach to talent management that "emphasizes a person's skills and competencies" rather than "degrees, job histories or job titles" when attracting, hiring, developing and redeploying talent.

The term skills-based organization extends that idea from hiring to the whole operating model: workforce planning, internal mobility, learning, and pay. There is no single standard definition, so organizations should state which talent processes they intend to make skills-based and which remain job-based.

sections.heading: How do talent processes change in a skills-based organization?

blocks.text: Each talent process swaps a proxy, such as a degree or a job title, for a skills requirement and a way to evidence it. The table is an original summary of the shift and the evidence each process then needs.

sections.heading: What does an organization need before it can be skills-based?

blocks.text: It needs a shared skills language and reliable evidence of skills. Without both, skills data is inconsistent and decisions based on it are hard to defend.

items: **A common skills language.** The WEF [Global Skills Taxonomy Adoption Toolkit](https://www3.weforum.org/docs/WEF_Global_Skills_Taxonomy_Adoption_Toolkit_2025.pdf) (January 2025) argues that a shared taxonomy enables clearer communication about the specific skills in demand. See [skills taxonomy](/glossary/skills-taxonomy) and [competency framework vs skills framework](/compare/competency-framework-vs-skills-framework).
**Defined skills requirements per role,** usually from job analysis, so each role lists the skills and levels it needs.
**Valid assessment** that produces evidence of skills, not self-ratings alone.
**Governance,** so the taxonomy, role requirements and skills records stay current. The WEF toolkit's third phase is to set up governance mechanisms for long-term sustainability.

sections.heading: What does skills-based hiring look like in government?

blocks.text: US federal hiring is a well-documented example. In 2020, [Executive Order 13932](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2020/07/01/2020-14337/modernizing-and-reforming-the-assessment-and-hiring-of-federal-job-candidates) directed that competitive service job postings be based on the specific skills and competencies required, and that agencies not rely solely on educational attainment to assess candidates. The Chance to Compete Act of 2024 (Public Law 118-188) followed, and OPM's [Merit Hiring Plan resources](https://www.opm.gov/policy-data-oversight/hiring-information/merit-hiring-plan-resources/) describe a Merit Hiring Plan issued on May 29, 2025.

OPM's FAQ on the [Rule of Many and skills-based hiring](https://www.opm.gov/policy-data-oversight/hiring-information/merit-hiring-plan-resources/rule-of-many-and-skills-based-hiring.pdf) defines skills-based hiring as "evaluating candidates based on their ability to perform the work using tools like job simulations, skills tests, or other structured assessments." Its February 2026 [guidance on self-reported assessments](https://www.opm.gov/policy-data-oversight/hiring-information/merit-hiring-plan-resources/guidance-on-the-use-of-self-reported-assessments.pdf) states that agencies must not use self-assessments to rate or rank applicants, except as OPM expressly authorizes, and must instead use validated technical and alternative assessments.

sections.heading: Why is skills evidence the hardest part?

blocks.text: Skills records are only useful if they are true, and most skills data starts as self-report or inference. The federal shift away from self-assessment for ranking illustrates the point: a claimed skill is a starting point, not evidence. Regulated organizations face the same test when a skills record is used to assign someone to safety-critical or customer-facing work.

Practical checks for any skills record: how the skill was evidenced (observed, tested, credentialed or self-reported), when, against which level definition, and by whom. These mirror the [rules of evidence](/glossary/rules-of-evidence) used in competency assessment, and the distinction between a skill and a [competency](/compare/competence-vs-competency) matters when the record is used for assurance.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry provides the structured layer a skills-based model depends on: skills and competencies defined in a framework, linked to roles, with assessment points that generate evidence rather than self-ratings. Each skills claim can then be traced to the assessment that supports it.

faqs.q: Does a skills-based organization get rid of job titles?
faqs.a: Usually not. Most organizations keep jobs for structure, pay and legal reasons, and describe each job as a set of skills. What changes is that decisions about hiring, moves and development are made against those skills and the evidence for them, rather than against the title or a credential alone.

faqs.q: Does skills-based hiring mean degrees no longer matter?
faqs.a: Not entirely. OPM's FAQ notes that its Rule of Many selection method does not remove qualification requirements such as minimum experience or education where these are legally required. In regulated roles, licenses and qualifications still apply. Skills-based approaches remove unnecessary proxies, not legal requirements.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a skills taxonomy and a skills-based organization?
faqs.a: A skills taxonomy is a structured list of skills with definitions and relationships. A skills-based organization is an operating model that uses skills as the basis for talent decisions. The taxonomy is one of its prerequisites, alongside role skill profiles, valid assessment and governance.

faqs.q: How large is the benefit of a skills-first approach?
faqs.a: Estimates vary and depend on assumptions. The WEF's Putting Skills First paper estimates, from data on 18 economies, that more than 100 million people could be added to the global talent pool through a skills-first approach. Organizations should measure their own results, such as quality of hire and time to proficiency.
